prime.problem: A tokenizer trained on mostly English will meet characters it never kept, like Korean or a rare symbol. If it has no plan for them, it either throws the text away as "unknown" or needs a vocabulary row for every character in Unicode.
prime.fits: You built byte-level BPE (minbpe, tiktoken's way) and saw how UTF-8 turns a character into 1–4 bytes. Llama 2's tokenizer runs the same BPE on characters instead, and uses those UTF-8 bytes only as a fallback.
expect: BPE on code points vs on bytes
prime.goal: Predict how a sentencepiece model encodes text it never saw, explain the id layout of its vocabulary, and train your own with Llama 2's settings.

attend: Where in the pipeline does sentencepiece turn text into bytes, and why only for some characters?
Why does the byte token for 0xEC get id 239 rather than 236?
What decides whether a character counts as "rare" enough to fall back to bytes?
With byte_fallback=False, why does a whole Korean word shrink to a single id, and can decode recover it?
Why does the dummy prefix make "world" match mid-sentence text but give " world" an extra piece?

must: sentencepiece merges code points, not bytes → a character outside the kept set has no piece → it must go somewhere: <unk> (text lost, decodes as " ⁇ ") or, with byte_fallback, its UTF-8 bytes (1–4 byte tokens, always round-trips)

character_coverage keeps the most frequent characters covering that share of the training text → characters from languages rare in the training data are dropped → those languages cost one byte token per UTF-8 byte (3 per Korean syllable) instead of merged pieces

Reserving 256 byte tokens costs vocabulary slots (256 of tok400's 400) → but guarantees any string can be encoded and decoded → which is why Llama 2 turns fallback on, and why tiktoken's bytes-first design gets the same guarantee for free
elevated: Specials come first (<unk>=0, <s>=1, </s>=2) → byte b lives at id b + 3 → code that assumes byte token = byte value is off by 3
add_dummy_prefix prepends a space → a word at the start of the text gets the same pieces as mid-sentence → but text that already starts with a space gets an extra ▁

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the two pipelines (tiktoken and sentencepiece) side by side, from text to ids, and mark where each one handles a character it never saw. Then say in 2–3 sentences what byte_fallback buys and what it costs.
checklist: tiktoken / minbpe: text → UTF-8 bytes → BPE on bytes, so nothing is ever unknown
sentencepiece: BPE on code points; only characters kept by character_coverage get pieces
a leftover character becomes <unk> (lost) or, with byte_fallback, its UTF-8 bytes
byte tokens sit after the 3 specials, so id = byte + 3
cost: 256 reserved ids, and rare-language text is long (3 byte tokens per Korean syllable)

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between running BPE on code points and running it on bytes, and why the code-point version needs a fallback plan at all.
answer: bytes: 256 base symbols cover every possible string, so there is always a way to encode
code points: over a hundred thousand possible characters; only the kept ones have pieces
anything else needs <unk> or byte fallback

retrieve.q: Walk through how tok400 encodes "hello 안녕하세요": which pieces appear, why the Korean looks the way it does, and how you get from 안 to id 239.
answer: dummy prefix and the space give ▁ pieces; hello becomes h, e, l, lo
Korean was never in the training text, so each syllable falls back to its 3 UTF-8 bytes (15 byte tokens)
안 starts with byte 0xEC = 236; 236 + 3 specials = 239
21 ids in total, and decode gives the string back exactly

retrieve.q: You're training a tokenizer for a mostly-English model that will occasionally see Korean. Compare byte_fallback=False, byte_fallback=True, and raising character_coverage to keep more characters. What does each cost?
answer: no fallback: the Korean becomes <unk> and is lost for good
fallback: always round-trips, but 3 byte tokens per syllable, and 256 ids reserved
higher coverage: more characters get their own row, but rare rows are barely trained, and unseen characters still need a plan

retrieve.q: Why does " world" encode to one more piece than "world" in tok400?
answer: add_dummy_prefix prepends a space to every input
"world" becomes " world" → ▁w, or, l, d
" world" becomes " world": the extra space is a lone ▁ in front

compare.q: Your GPT-4 tokenizer (bytes first, regex split) vs Llama 2's sentencepiece tokenizer (code points first, byte fallback): what is fundamentally different about the base symbols, which design choice makes each one handle unseen text, and how does each fail?
answer: GPT-4: 256 byte symbols are the base, merged upward; unseen text is just bytes, with no special path
Llama 2: characters are the base; bytes appear only for dropped characters, and ids are offset by the specials
both round-trip any string (Llama 2 only because byte_fallback is on)
failure: sentencepiece without fallback loses text as <unk>; both bloat rare languages

compare.q: That card argued raw code points and raw bytes both fail as a vocabulary. How does sentencepiece combine the two to get around each one's problem?
answer: raw code points: too many (about 150k) and they keep changing, so keep only the common ones
raw bytes: sequences too long, so use them only for rare characters
result: common text is short, and rare text is long but never lost

predict.q: The toy text has no digits at all. With split_digits=True and byte_fallback=True, what pieces and ids does tok400 give for "2024"?
predict.answer: ['▁', '<0x32>', '<0x30>', '<0x32>', '<0x34>'] with ids [362, 53, 51, 53, 55]. The digits were never seen, so they aren't in the vocabulary and fall back to bytes. Each is a single ASCII byte (0x32 = 50 for "2"), so the id is 50 + 3 = 53. split_digits never gets a chance to matter here, because there are no digit pieces to split. (Scratch run with tok400.)

apply.task: Retrain tok400 with character_coverage=0.99 instead of 0.99995 and encode "BPE, Kudo" with both models. List which characters were dropped from the vocabulary and why those ones.
apply.done: At 0.99995 you get 7 pieces (▁ BP E , ▁ Ku do); at 0.99 you get 9, with B, E, , and K as byte tokens (<0x42>, <0x45>, <0x2C>, <0x4B>). The dropped set is , / B E K: 5 characters seen once each, and 498 / 503 = 0.990 still meets the 0.99 target.
apply.hint: Count each character in toy.txt with collections.Counter and sort by count. sentencepiece rejects a coverage below 0.98.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 21 ids, the 239, or the "2024" bytes?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the byte ids are offset, or why the no-fallback model splits "hello" differently?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: character_coverage → which characters are dropped, or dropped characters → longer sequences for rare languages?
Would you pick sentencepiece or tiktoken for a new model, and what would change your mind?
What will you revisit before the vocabulary-size card?
